name: Damiana extract (Turnera diffusa)

lead: Damiana is a shrub used in teas and liqueurs and sold as an herbal supplement. Some supplement users take it as a natural anti-aromatase to support testosterone, aiming for slightly lower estrogen conversion and a leaner, more muscular look.
A 2008 laboratory study reported that flavonoids in damiana, such as pinocembrin and acacetin, inhibit aromatase. No human trial of damiana alone on estrogen or appearance was found.

paras: It is taken as a tea, tincture or capsule, often inside combination hormone-support products. Users do not describe a clear timeline.
Safety data are limited in the sources reviewed. Products may contain false damiana (Turnera ulmifolia), and combination products make effects hard to attribute.

angle.text: Damiana is a traditional herb that supplement users take as a natural anti-aromatase, aiming for slightly lower estrogen and a leaner look. A 2008 lab study found anti-aromatase constituents; human trials of the extract alone are absent.

lead: Damiana (Turnera diffusa) is a small shrub native to southern Texas, Mexico, Central and South America and the Caribbean. It has been used in Mexican liqueurs, herbal teas and smoking blends, and in 19th-century patent medicines promoted as an aphrodisiac [1].

In bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation circles it is mentioned as a natural aromatase inhibitor. A 2008 paper in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology reported anti-aromatase activity of damiana constituents, and Wikipedia lists the flavonoids pinocembrin and acacetin as the compounds involved [2][3]. These findings come from laboratory work; no human trial testing damiana for estrogen levels or appearance was identified.

paras: The plant contains flavonoids such as apigenin and acacetin, plus terpenoids, phenolics and cyanogenic glycosides. As of 2006 the constituents responsible for the whole herb's effects had not been identified [1]. A 2020 review notes that acacetin, a flavone also present in damiana, has been studied for anticancer, anti-inflammatory and other pharmacological effects in cell and animal models [4]. A 2014 review covers the ethnobotany and chemistry of the genus Turnera with a focus on damiana [5].

A 2008 study reported anti-aromatase activity of constituents from damiana [2]. Wikipedia's aromatase inhibitor page notes that damiana extract is reported to suppress aromatase activity, but flags the claims as needing better sourcing [3]. A 1998 screening study found estrogen- and progestin-receptor binding in a number of herbs tested in human cancer cells, which is a different mechanism from aromatase inhibition [6].

Many plants sold as damiana are in fact Turnera ulmifolia, or false damiana, a related species with different chemistry, though this mislabelling is mostly found in horticultural sales [1]. A homeopathic and herbal combination product labelled for low energy lists damiana among its ingredients [7].

No studies found on damiana alone for aromatase inhibition, estrogen levels or appearance. Related human research tested multi-ingredient products: a 2001 trial of the ArginMax supplement (which contains damiana among other ingredients) in female sexual function [8], and a 2001 study of a South American herbal preparation in overweight patients, which reported weight loss and delayed gastric emptying [9]. These cannot isolate damiana's contribution.
